These clinical features — including the “stuck-on” appearance, greasy (verrucous or waxy) surface, lack of inflammation, absence of symptoms (no pruritus, pain, or bleeding), and characteristic cerebriform pattern on dermatoscopy — are classic for seborrheic keratosis. The histopathology confirms hyperkeratosis and horn cysts, which are hallmark microscopic findings of seborrheic keratosis. Age-appropriateness (common after age 50), benign course, and lack of concerning features (e.g., asymmetry, irregular borders, color variegation, rapid growth, ulceration, or melanocytic atypia on dermatoscopy or biopsy) further support this diagnosis and reliably exclude malignancies such as melanoma, basal cell carcinoma, or squamous cell carcinoma. The absence of systemic symptoms and unremarkable review of systems also argues against paraneoplastic or inflammatory etiologies.

DIAGNOSIS: Seborrheic keratosis
